PNG decoder conformance

Every decoder below was run over the same 696 small PNG files from difftest-png, each one built to test one rule of the PNG specification or one behavior on which some decoder deviates. Run 2026-10-28T00:04:50+00:00 on Linux x86_64.

Each result is rated under each lens: pass, should (the specification says a decoder should do otherwise, e.g. recover a recoverable fault instead of rejecting the image) or must (a requirement is broken: wrong pixels, an invalid file accepted, a valid file rejected, a crash, a hang, a memory error). Warnings never count against a decoder. Running out of memory counts like a crash: a file should be rejected with an error, and a decoder that instead exhausts its host hands every program that opens untrusted images a denial of service. Pixels are compared as 16-bit RGBA with no color management; color under fully transparent pixels and the 8-bit reduction of 16-bit images are recorded as properties, not failures. Validators (pngcheck) are judged on a different question: whether each file conforms to the specification. Some files a decoder must still display do not conform, for example one with a chunk name the specification reserves.

Two editions of the specification matter: the second (ISO/IEC 15948:2003; PNG 1.0 and 1.1 count as the second) and the third (W3C, 2025). A lens is an edition's text plus the extensions: the W3C registered extensions, Apple's iDOT, and under the second edition the chunks the third edition added (APNG, cICP, mDCV, cLLI, eXIf). Every result is rated through both lenses separately; each table has a checkbox per edition, and shows the ticked ones. There is no single verdict: following one edition rather than the other is not a defect. The two ratings differ only where the texts contradict each other, which they do in one place: a palette index past the end of PLTE is an error in the second edition and renders opaque black in the third.

Not tested: animation frames after the default image, color management (gAMA, cHRM, iCCP, sRGB, cICP, sBIT), encoders, performance. Passing every test means the suite is incomplete, not that the decoder is perfect.

Human disclaimer

The results likely contain errors, or decisions which can be argued with. Regardless, I did take greater-than-usual care to make this meaningful. The code is probably vibeslop, and I haven't read a single line. But, the decisions here came from several rounds of Matt Pocock's grill-me Skill and at least four separate essays I wrote while trying to keep Claude Opus 5.5 on track, alongside several rounds of adversarial checking from GPT-6 Astra and from Claude Fable 5.1. I had to "push back" quite a lot to get past the AI's boneheaded decisions.

My conclusion: Parsing PNGs is a Minefield. A modern JSON comparison is coming Soon™, don't worry :)

The first four rows are must-violations and the fifth should-violations. silent: the column accepted a file that does not conform and said nothing about it; a count, not a violation. strict: a validator rejected a file that conforms, over a name a strict reading of the naming rules may flag (iDOT's unregistered public name); recorded, not a violation.

chunky_png, pillow and upng return at most 8 bits per sample. All of them keep the high byte of a 16-bit sample and drop the low byte.

Every decoder preserves the color under fully transparent pixels, except chunky_png, pngjs and wuffs: they zero it under a tRNS color key.
